zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check only, after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima, with Taichi Aida; source licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). Transcription choices and English review notes here are this reviewer's scan-based work, not a reproduction of the headword dataset.

lines.note: Joo denotes obstinacy or a fixed opinion. Joo wo haru illustrates insisting on one's position; the initial I and its caroned o are retained from the scan.

runs.text: Ter mão ẽ ſua opinião, ou ſer teimoſo. ¶

lines.note: Explains holding firmly to one's opinion or being stubborn. The next Japanese phrase begins Iǒ- at the line end; ẽ remains an unexpanded nasal abbreviation.
Completes joo no kowai hito, a stubborn person. Teimoſo is a single printed word, not the OCR's tei moſo; afer- continues below.

runs.text: rado a ſeu parecer. ¶ Item, Nos liuros

lines.note: Completes aferrado a seu parecer, firmly attached to one's view. Item introduces a different sense found in books.

runs.text: ſe toma por amor, ou piedade.

lines.note: The written usage is love or compassion. This sense belongs to the same joo entry, rather than to the following old-person homophone.
Joo here means an old person, toshiyori. The visible circumflex is retained, despite the different mark on the surrounding obstinacy entry.

runs.text: Cinza em que ſe deſfaz a braſa, ou car-

lines.note: Another joo denotes ash into which glowing coal breaks down. The circumflex is visible; car- begins carvão on the next line.

runs.text: uão aceſo ainda que fica de baixo algum fogo,

lines.note: Completes carvão and explains that the coal may still contain some fire underneath. De baixo remains the printed two-word form.
The explanation adds remaining embers. Oki mina joo ni natta says the embers have all turned to ash, with the circumflex repeated in jôni.

runs.text: a braſa esta deſfeita toda em cinza. ¶

lines.note: Completes the statement that all the embers have become ash. No begins a Portuguese explanation continued by chanoyuu; its upright type is retained rather than changed solely because it is Portuguese.

The Portuguese says that in chanoyuu one uses sumi nadareta for the subsiding embers. Chanoyǔ is upright, while Sumi nadareta is visibly italic in this impression; both are Japanese expressions embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: as braſas ja baixas, & des feitas quaſi ẽ cinza.

lines.note: Explains the expression as embers already low and almost reduced to ash. The gap before ẽ is visible; the separate des feitas is retained rather than normalized.
Joo here means a padlock. Joo wo orosu means fastening or putting on the lock, with the Portuguese object supplied below.
Completes lançar cadeado and contrasts opening it, joo wo akuru. The damaged but identifiable Iǒuo replaces the OCR's Muo.
Completes cadeado, the object of abrir. This short row belongs to the lock example.
Jooban is the guard of a fortress, explicitly shiro no ban. The missing initial I in the OCR is present in the scan.

runs.text: Vigia ordinaria, & que não ſe troca.

lines.note: This jooban is a standing or regular guard that is not replaced in rotation. It is distinct from the fortress-guard sense immediately above.
Joobita describes something excellent or accomplished. The following examples apply it first to a person's bearing, then to hospitality.
Joobita hito is a person of honourable or excellent character. The damaged medial y of Laya is supported by its surviving strokes; OCR Laga does not match the impression.
Completes the description of excellence in person and conduct. The mark after trato is a paragraph sign, not q; fu- begins furumai below.
Completes joobita furumai, splendid hospitality or a magnificent feast. The Portuguese explicitly gives banquete, distinguishing this example's sense from personal bearing.
Joobitaki is identified simply as a bird of that name. The scan reads Aueſinha, repairing OCR Aueſmha; the definition does not itself supply a modern species name.
Joobon is a high class or grade, explained by ue no shina. The Portuguese introduces a class or order of excellent things.
Completes the high-grade definition with excellent and supreme things. It belongs to joobon, not the next volume-related entry.

runs.text: Primeira parte, ou tomo dalgum liuro.

lines.note: Joobu is the first part or volume of a book. The source has the initial I omitted by OCR.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Suprema, ou primeira parte, como

lines.note: Adds the highest or first portion in a spatial division. The scan supports primeira, not the OCR's nasalized prãmeira.
The region of the air illustrates this upper-portion sense. Regiam is retained as the printed historical spelling.
Joobun is an upper portion, explicitly ue no bun. It is a separate headword from the following report-to-a-superior sense.
The dictionary prefers shoobun for making something heard by, or reporting to, a superior. Meliùs is italic editorial apparatus; the alternative Japanese form remains roman.

runs.text: dizer a peßoa alta, & nobre, como Cubǒ,

lines.note: Continues reporting to a high-ranking person, with Kuboo as an example. Cubǒ is a Japanese title embedded in the Portuguese explanation; its visibly italic type is retained.
Yacata adds another lordly title, visibly italic as a whole rather than the OCR's split styling. Joobun ni tassuru illustrates addressing such a superior; Fa- begins falar.
Completes falar a estas pessoas, speaking to those high-ranking people. The two long-s forms in peſſoas are retained.

runs.text: Ouuir de peßoa alta, & nobre o que

lines.note: This joobun is hearing what a high-ranking person says, contrasting with reporting to one in the preceding entry. The circumflex is retained from the printed headword.
Completes the hearing gloss: what the superior says or commands. It is not a continuation of the earlier speaking-to-a-superior example.
Joobutsu means becoming a Buddha, hotoke ni naru. The embedded Fotoque in the Portuguese explanation is printed italic here; the final t in Iǒbut is historical checked-coda notation.
Adds being saved as the Portuguese interpretation of attaining Buddhahood. It completes the preceding religious entry.
A homophonous joobutsu denotes a conveyance, norimono, described as a kind of litter. Its circumflex contrasts with the preceding religious headword's caron.

runs.text: que leuão homẽs aos ombros, ou nas mãos.

lines.note: The litter is carried by men on their shoulders or in their hands. Homẽs retains the nasal abbreviation in the scan.

runs.text: Mundo ſuperior, ou ſobre os Ce-

lines.note: Jookai is the upper world, marked as Buddhist vocabulary by upright Bup. The initial I corrects OCR F; Ce- begins Ceos.
Completes Ceos and gives jookai gekai, the upper and lower worlds. The Portuguese pairs heavens and earth.
Completes the contrast between the higher world and this lower one. The demonstrative eſte refers to the present world.
This jookai denotes pure precepts, explained by kiyoi kaimon. The scan's large Q is clear and corrects OCR Giyoi.
Completes the definition of the law or commandments as pure and right. It belongs to the precept entry rather than the upper-world homophone.
Joochaku means arriving after going up, nobori tsuku. The Portuguese begins arrival at a place conventionally described as upward.

runs.text: gar em reſpeito do qual ſe diz ſubir, como ao

lines.note: Completes lugar and explains the relational use of 'go up', not necessarily a literal climb. The scan reads como ao rather than OCR cõmo co.
The capital, Miaco, is the example of a destination one goes up to. This completes the preceding arrival definition.
Joochuu is inside a fortress, explicitly shiro no uchi. The checked headword keeps its two visible vowel marks.

runs.text: Iǒ, chǔ, gue. Vye, naca, xita.

lines.note: Joo, chuu, ge are upper, middle and lower, explicitly ue, naka and shita. The Portuguese ſu- begins ſuprema; the initial I was misread as l in OCR.
Completes the three grades: supreme, middle and lowest. The source's meoã is retained with the tilde over its final a; Item adds a spatial paraphrase.
Completes em cima and gives in the middle and below. This is the spatial use of the same three terms.
Jooko is the commander of a fortress. The Portuguese dalgũa keeps its visible nasal sign.

runs.text: Bom reino. i, Onde ha riquezas, &

lines.note: Jookoku is a good or prosperous country, explained as one with riches. The explanatory i, belongs to the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Completes the prosperity gloss with good things. It belongs to jookoku rather than the following physical-vigour entry.
Jookon denotes a good, strong natural constitution. The initial is I, not the OCR long s.
Are wa jookon no hito ja means that person has a strong constitution. The scan prints Aquelle as one word, not OCR A quelle.
Completes the description of that man as well constituted and strong. It is the predicate of the preceding Portuguese sentence.
Joku aku concerns impurity and evil, explained by nigoru and aku. The Portuguese calls it wickedness or sin; pecca- continues below.
Completes peccado and illustrates joku aku sekai, an impure world. Immũdo preserves the printed nasal abbreviation.
Jokuketsu is corrupted blood, literally nigotta chi. The scan supports initial I rather than OCR r; final t is the historical checked-coda notation.
Joodaku denotes hearing and assenting, with uketamawari and ukegoo as explanations. The initial I corrects OCR F, and both circumflexes remain as printed.

runs.text: conſentir com o que lhe dizem.

lines.note: Completes the definition: consenting to what one is told. It belongs to joodaku, not the historical-age entry below.
Joodai is an ancient age described as peaceful and flourishing. Antigua is the printed historical form.
Ima wa joodai ni natta says the present has become like that flourishing ancient age. The Portuguese translation continues on the next row.

runs.text: ou idade como a antigua florente, &c.

lines.note: Completes the comparison of the present age with the flourishing ancient one. Antigua, not OCR amigua, is supported by the scan.
Joodan is the highest level, literally ue no dan. The following extension describes an elevated seating place.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Lugar mais alto que ſe faz no Za-

lines.note: Adds a raised place made in a zashiki for the lord. The embedded word begins with a visible capital Z, Za-, not the OCR's lowercase z. Za- is the first printed fragment of the embedded Japanese room-name Zaxiqui.

Completes Zaxiqui across the line break and explains that the raised place is for the lord to occupy. The Japanese room-name remains in the italic type actually printed here. The opening xiqui completes the preceding Za-; both fragments remain italic as printed.
Joodoo is attaining the way, doo wo joozuru. The Portuguese begins becoming or reaching Buddhahood; the damaged initial of Fazerſe is F, not OCR P.
Completes the attainment gloss as reaching the dignity of a Buddha. Fotoque is a Japanese word embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation.

Joodo is the pure land, explained by qiyoi cuni. The Portuguese gloss proceeds from clean land to paradise; the explanatory i, is retained where the punctuation is locally ink-filled and irregular, rather than inventing an additional mark.
Completes the phrase as the Buddha's paradise. Fotoque is embedded in the Portuguese gloss, not a separate Japanese example.
This separate joodo is explained by ue no nori and glossed simply as law. The initial I corrects OCR F; the wording is retained without imposing a more specific modern doctrinal sense.

Joodoshuu denotes adherents of the Joodo school. The embedded school-name Iǒdo is upright within the italic Portuguese. I retain the baseline's capital I: its tall stem is interrupted by a white break rather than showing the small, separate dot of the neighboring lowercase i; the damaged impression makes capitalization a minor caveat.
Joohakumai is very white, thoroughly prepared rice. Arroz corrects the OCR's Anroz, with the description completed by pilado below.
Pilado specifies rice well pounded or milled. This short row completes the preceding rice definition.
Joohai means the higher-ranking people, ue no tomogara. The Portuguese prin- begins principais.
Completes principais and gives joohai wa gehai wo awaremu, the higher ranks showing compassion toward the lower ranks.

runs.text: Os grandes tem miſericordia dos pequenos.

lines.note: Translates the preceding social comparison: the great have mercy on the small. The historical unaccented tem is retained.

runs.text: Ao longo, ou a par da

lines.note: Joohen is the vicinity of a fortress, shiro no hotori. The Portuguese describes being alongside it, with the noun completed on the next row.
Completes the description of being beside the fortress. The scan prints fortaleza as one word, not OCR forta leza.

runs.text: Bom eſcriuão, ou boa letra, ou boa mão

lines.note: Joohitsu denotes a good writer, fine handwriting, or a good writing hand. These alternatives are supplied directly by the Portuguese definition.
Completes boa mão pera escrever, skill at writing. This is part of the joohitsu definition.
Johitsu is assistance with writing, literally tasuke fude. Fude means brush; the visible f and the writing gloss support fude rather than OCR ſude.
Joojuu means always or continually. The initial I is present despite its loss in OCR; co- begins koto in the example.
Completes joojuu fudan no koto nari, something constant or habitual. The Portuguese renders it as an ordinary or regular matter.
Joojuugi is everyday clothing. De cote supplies the habitual sense; the Japanese example ends with the first part of suru.
Completes suru and translates wearing a garment regularly. Trazer is used of wearing, not merely transporting, the clothing.
Joojuumotsu denotes something constant or ordinary. The final t remains the dictionary's checked-coda spelling.
Joogoo is something usual or recurring, explained by tsune tsune. The first long-o mark is a caron and the final one a circumflex.
Joogo is a drinker or someone fond of alcoholic drink. The dictionary's vinho is retained without narrowing it to grape wine.
This joogo is a funnel. Joogo de sake wo tsugu illustrates pouring drink through one; the headword begins with I, not OCR l.
Translates the funnel example: pour the drink through a funnel. It belongs to the implement sense, not the preceding drinker sense.
Jogon is verbal assistance or advice, explained by tasuke kotoba. The Portuguese definition continues into an example spanning the page boundary.
Conſelho, advice, repairs the OCR's final e. Goxǒguini begins an example about speaking during go and shogi; jo- continues as gon at the top of f293, while the bottom gon is only the catchword.
